title: A Case of the Mondays: Hot Seats, Cease-and-Desist Letters, and a Python's Worth of Perspective
paragraphs: Nothing says 'we are ready for a real football game' quite like a week dominated by a jersey number dispute in Baton Rouge, but here we are. Before the Commanders even sniff Week 1, the biggest Jayden Daniels headline of the weekend had nothing to do with Washington at all. LSU fans reportedly had a strong reaction to an image of Daniels on the video board during the Clemson game, which is a sentence that requires no further embellishment because it is already perfect. The man won a Heisman there, issued a cease-and-desist over his own retired-ish number being handed to a sophomore corner, and now gets booed on the big screen at his alma mater. Some guys just can't win, even when they've already won the biggest trophy college football hands out.

Meanwhile in Washington, the actual football team is doing what it does best this time of year: generating a thousand hot takes with zero snaps played. Riggo's Rag alone published enough hot-seat, mock-draft, and 'last stand' content this week to make you think the season already happened and went badly, when in reality nobody has even kicked off yet. Dan Quinn is reportedly facing renewed job-security speculation with Mike Tomlin's name getting kicked around as a shadow looming over his future, which feels like an odd thing to be discussing before Daniels has thrown a single real pass this year. Adam Peters, for his part, sounds like a man trying to stay above it all, quietly noting the team has real cap space partly because of extensions still to come, plural, with his own quarterback presumably at the top of that list.

The Commanders did make one move you can actually hang your hat on: Van Jefferson is back, signing to the practice squad less than two weeks after getting let go in roster cuts. It is the football equivalent of breaking up and getting back together before the group chat even stops buzzing about it. John Keim notes the receiver room simply has more depth and variety than it did last year, which, given how 2025 went at that position, is a bar so low you could trip over it walking backwards. Elsewhere, Drake Jackson's release with an injury settlement quietly closes a chapter that never really opened, and Ben Sinnott apparently used his final-chance moment to take a shot at former offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury, which is the kind of thing you do when you have genuinely nothing left to lose.

There is, encouragingly, a defense-shaped silver lining buzzing around Ashburn. Daronte Jones' backstory, a coach who slept in his car with a pet python and nearly quit twice before landing his current gig, is the kind of story that makes you root for a coordinator regardless of scheme. His answer for a shaky cornerback group seems to hinge less on individual talent and more on pressure and disguise, which John Keim's reporting suggests is basically the whole ballgame: good pressure, good defense; no pressure, watch out. Add in K'Lavon Chaisson working his way back to practice and the front seven getting talked up as this team's actual backbone, and you have the first genuinely optimistic through-line of the offseason. It is still September, so optimism is legally required to be handled with oven mitts.

Nationally, nobody is exactly picking up the phone for the Commanders. Beat reporters keep circling back to how low the outside expectations are for Washington this year, tempered only by the reminder that the same thing happened the last two seasons and it did not exactly predict the outcome. CBS Sports even floated the Commanders among the possible last-place finishers in their division for 2026, the kind of preseason exercise that exists purely to be screenshotted and mocked in December. Ben Standig's take feels like the sanest one in the building: the concerns are real, the O-line is concerning, Jayden needs to stay healthy, all true, but only the deepest teams can survive several catastrophes hitting at once, and that is a fair, boring, grown-up way to feel about a team nobody outside the Beltway believes in yet.

Around the rest of the league, the preseason parlor game of 'who is on the hot seat' is of course not just a Washington pastime, it is basically the sport's national anthem every September, and this year is no different anywhere else in the NFC East, where the Eagles are reportedly still figuring out their offensive identity while leaning on a defense expected to be really good. Zach Ertz, of all people, is being connected to a storybook reunion with Philadelphia, which would be a fittingly strange twist for a division that never does anything the simple way. Stefon Diggs trade rumors, meanwhile, are apparently circulating with such little grounding in reality that Commanders fans have every right to just laugh them off entirely.

Now, the part of the column I genuinely look forward to writing every week: Virginia football, viewed from the President's Box, which is to say viewed while eating catered food my wife's job gets us for free, because apparently that's a perk of marrying someone smarter than me. The Cavaliers hosted NC State at Scott Stadium and did not just win, they dismantled the Wolfpack 34-8, which meant I spent a Saturday afternoon watching my team dominate while balancing a plate of something significantly better than stadium nachos. There is a very specific joy in watching a blowout unfold from a comfortable chair with a full stomach, and I will not apologize for it, mostly because the Commanders have not given me many comparable Saturdays lately.

UVA now gets to enjoy a tune-up against Norfolk State before things get more serious, and frankly after a 34-8 win I am fully prepared to keep showing up to that box on a purely scientific basis: it keeps working. Around the sport, the results were mostly what you'd expect from an early slate stacked with overmatched opponents, Ohio State cruising past Ball State, Oregon needing much less trouble than that scoreline suggests against Boise State, and Miami putting up 45 on Stanford in a way that makes you wonder if the Cardinal accidentally scheduled themselves into the wrong decade. None of that changes my Saturday plans, though. I'll be back in that box next home game, plate in hand, rooting for the Cavaliers and quietly hoping the Commanders can borrow some of that same energy before Sunday rolls around again.

corpus.text: National Football League Players Association (NFLPA) announced that Matt Taylor will join the organization as Chief Communications Officer, effective September 8. Taylor served as a Vice President at Heller, a leading strategic communications firm, where he advised clients navigating complex issues across a range of industries. Taylor also led football communications for the Miami Dolphins, and served in communications positions in the front offices of the Indianapolis Colts and Washington Commanders.
